headline: High risk of shared-workspace prompt injection and data leakage; Gemini CLI’s MCP and filesystem access amplify CrewAI’s shared-memory orchestration.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: CrewAI can read/write the host working directory and uses shared memory by default, while Gemini CLI reads repo files and can use user-configured MCP tools. That creates a plausible content-to-instruction bridge if one agent writes attacker-controlled text that the other later parses. The pathway is interaction-based and not blocked by default isolation.
conditions: IF CrewAI writes untrusted text into the shared working directory and Gemini CLI later ingests that file as instructions, injection is possible.
IF Gemini CLI is configured with an MCP server that exposes tool outputs back into CrewAI-readable files, the bridge strengthens.
mitigations: Separate the agents into different directories.
Disable file-based handoff between agents.
Require human review of any file one agent writes before the other reads it.
Run both agents in containers with distinct mounts.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to all inter-agent artifacts.

B_data_leakage.rationale: CrewAI handles developer-passed crew data and API keys, and Gemini CLI touches repo files, cwd files, and shell environment. Because both can read/write the same host filesystem and Gemini CLI can send context to a third-party model API, sensitive data can flow from CrewAI-managed artifacts into Gemini’s outbound requests in default setups.
conditions: IF CrewAI stores secrets or sensitive crew inputs in the shared workspace and Gemini CLI reads those files, leakage occurs.
IF Gemini CLI forwards those files into generativelanguage.googleapis.com, the data leaves the local environment.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared workspace.
Use separate OS users for each agent.
Restrict Gemini CLI to non-sensitive directories.
Rotate any API keys exposed to shared files.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent workspace ACLs.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, and subprocess spawning; Gemini CLI also modifies git state while CrewAI can write the same host working directory. In a shared repo or cwd, concurrent edits can clobber files or corrupt git state, and there is no built-in cross-agent locking in either profile.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same directory, write conflicts can occur.
IF Gemini CLI commits or rewrites git state while CrewAI writes files concurrently, repository corruption or lost work is plausible.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate checkout.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Disable git-mutating actions for Gemini CLI during parallel runs.
Use a lock file around shared directories.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: CrewAI’s role-playing/shared-memory outputs can become inputs to Gemini CLI, which has tool approval and can act on shell or MCP tools. If Gemini treats CrewAI-generated text as authoritative, errors or fabricated facts can cascade into commands or file edits. The pair lacks an explicit verification boundary in the profiles.
conditions: IF Gemini CLI consumes CrewAI output without a verification step, downstream actions may be based on false premises.
IF CrewAI emits unverified summaries that Gemini CLI turns into shell commands or MCP calls, the cascade becomes operational.
mitigations: Require a verification step before Gemini acts on CrewAI output.
Have a human approve any command derived from another agent’s text.
Limit CrewAI to drafting, not executing.
Log source-to-action traces for each handoff.
requires-engineering: implement structured, typed inter-agent messages.

E_compliance.rationale: CrewAI explicitly handles developer-passed crew data and Gemini CLI handles repo files, cwd files, and shell environment; both may therefore process sensitive material under different retention and vendor paths. The profiles do not document aligned residency, retention, or subject-rights controls, so compliance mismatch is plausible even though no specific regulated class is named.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in the shared workspace, the two agents may process it under different vendor and retention regimes.
IF organizational policy requires a single residency or retention model, the pair may violate it.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair’s workspace.
Review vendor terms before use.
Use separate environments for regulated and unregulated work.
Disable logging of sensitive prompts and files.
requires-engineering: document and enforce retention/residency policy.
